subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Empiricism: Knowledge from Experience
description: One-minute skill: Empiricism: Knowledge from Experience.

hook.text: John Locke said the mind starts as a blank slate – all knowledge comes from sensory experience.

buildup.text: Empiricism: the view that knowledge comes from observation and experience, not from innate ideas or pure reason.

discovery.text: It's the foundation of modern science. Don't theorize in a vacuum — go look, measure, test.

twist.text: But empiricism has limits. You can't observe mathematical truths, logical laws, or ethics.

climax.text: Hume's fork: meaningful statements are either empirical or analytic. Everything else is meaningless.

punchline.text: See it, test it, measure it. If you can't, ask why you believe it.

quiz.question: What is the core claim of empiricism?
options: Knowledge comes from observation and experience

details.summary: Empiricism holds that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience and observation rather than innate ideas or pure reason. It is the philosophical foundation of the scientific method and experimental research.
details.whyItMatters: Empiricism grounds knowledge in observable evidence, preventing the acceptance of claims based purely on authority, tradition, or wishful thinking.
takeaways: Knowledge derives from observation and experience
John Locke, David Hume, and Francis Bacon were key empiricists
Empiricism underlies the scientific demand for evidence

faq.question: How does empiricism differ from rationalism as a theory of knowledge?
faq.answer: Empiricism says knowledge comes from experience and observation. Rationalism says some knowledge comes from reason alone, independent of experience. Most modern science uses both, but prioritizes empirical evidence as the final arbiter.

faq.question: What are the main limitations of empiricism as a philosophy?
faq.answer: Senses can be deceived, some knowledge seems to precede experience like mathematical truths, and the problem of induction means past observations cannot logically guarantee future patterns. Pure empiricism needs supplementation.
